blocks.text: Moses forbids the raven to the Jews למינו, after its kind, or after its species, as he does certain other birds in the list of the unclean. And, as R. Selomo notes, when after its kind is added to the name of a bird, יש באותו המין שאין דומין זה לזה לא כמראיהם ולא בשמותיהם וכולן מין אחד, it has species unlike in form and name, which are nevertheless referred to one kind. But we shall show below that this is hardly well founded. Still, if you ask for the species of ravens, there may be referred to it the crow, the graculus [jackdaw], the jackdaw, the magpie, and even the starling, if one believes Baal Hatturim, who relies on a Cabbalistic argument: namely, that the words עורב למינו, the raven after its kind, and the word זרזר, that is, starling, are ἰσόψηφα [isopsēpha]. For both amount to 414. The Arabs in Damir describe the species of the raven thus: والغربان اربعة اجناس اسود حالك وابلق ومطرف ببياض لطيف الجرم ياكل الحب واسود طاووسي براق الريش ورجلاه بلون المرجان يعرف بالزاغ [wa-l-ghirbān arbaʿat ajnās aswad ḥālik wa-ablaq wa-muṭarraf bi-bayāḍ laṭīf al-jirm yaʾkul al-ḥabb wa-aswad ṭāwūsī barrāq al-rīsh wa-rijlāhu bi-lawn al-marjān yuʿraf bi-l-zāgh], There are four species of ravens. 1. The perfectly black (this is the raven properly so called). 2. The pied, or mixed of black and white (I understand the crow which in our vernacular we call the palliata [hooded]). 3. The one that has white extremities, slender in body, feeding on grains (that is, the σπερμολόγος [spermologos] crow). 4. The peacock-like black one, with shining plumage and coral-coloured feet, which is called the magpie. That the Arabs [col. 203] refer the crow to the raven kind is clearest from the fact that they consistently call the plant κορωνόπους [korōnopous] رجل الغراب [rijl al-ghurāb] raven's foot.

One of the princes of Midian was called עורב Oreb, that is, raven. And the place in which he was slain by the Ephraimites is the Rock of Oreb, Iudic. VII, 25. and Esa. X, 26. Likewise Κόρακος πέτρη [Korakos petrē], the rock of Corax, or of the raven, was a place on Ithaca, at which ὁ Κόραξ κυνηγῶν ἀπὸ τῆς πέτρας πεσῶν ἐτελεύτησε [ho Korax kynēgōn apo tēs petras pesōn eteleutēse], a certain hunter Corax (that is, named raven) died after falling from the rock. So the old Scholiast on the verse of Homer, Odyss. 13:
Παρ' Κόρακος πέτρῃ, ἐπί τε κρήνῃ Ἀρεθούσῃ. [Par' Korakos petrē, epi te krēnē Arethousē.]
